title: Year-Round Exterior Care Calendar for North Florida
description: A season-by-season exterior maintenance schedule for North Central Florida homes: washing, caulking, sun-side touch-ups, and planning the next repaint.
h1: A Year-Round Exterior Care Calendar for North Central Florida
heroIntro: Small tasks spread across the year cost far less than an emergency repaint. This calendar matches each job to the season when it does the most good in our climate.

sections.h2: Why a calendar works better than waiting for damage
body: Every season in North Central Florida attacks a house differently. Spring coats it in pine and oak pollen. Summer brings daily storms, high humidity, and the heaviest UV of the year. Fall is the driest, mildest stretch and the best time to fix things. Winter is short, but cold snaps and heavy dew still matter for wood and caulk.

A paint job does not usually fail all at once; it fails at its weakest points, such as a cracked caulk joint, a window sill that holds water, or a south wall that chalks faster than the rest. Catching those spots early is what a home exterior maintenance schedule is for. The calendar below assumes a typical single-family home with painted siding or stucco, wood or composite trim, and some fencing or decking.

sections.h2: Spring (March to May): wash and inspect
body: Once the pollen has mostly fallen, usually by late spring, wash the house. Doing it earlier just means doing it twice. Use a low-pressure soft wash with a cleaner suited to the surface; our guide on removing Florida pollen stains explains why pollen left on a wall turns into a stain and a food source for mildew.
bullets: Wash siding, soffits, and trim, working from the bottom up and rinsing from the top down.
Look for green or black growth on shaded walls and treat it with a mildewcide.
Walk the perimeter and note any peeling, blistering, or cracked caulk while the surface is clean.
Check that sprinklers are not spraying the walls before summer irrigation ramps up.
Spring is also a good window to stain fences and decks before summer heat.

sections.h2: Summer (June to September): monitor and manage water
body: Summer is the hardest season on coatings and the least comfortable time to paint a full exterior, so the job here is mostly observation and water control. After a few heavy storms, step outside and watch where the water actually goes.

If something cannot wait, such as a failed sill or a peeling door, do small repairs early in the morning once the dew has dried, and finish well before the afternoon thunderstorms build. Fresh latex paint that gets rained on before it sets can streak or wash out, so check the radar before you open the can. Hurricane season also runs through these months, so it is a good time to confirm that shutters, gutters, and loose trim are secure.
bullets: Clear gutters and make sure downspouts carry water away from the foundation and off the siding.
Look for splash-back staining along the bottom of walls and add gravel or extensions where needed.
Watch for bubbling paint or swollen trim, which are signs of moisture getting into the wall.
Trim shrubs and branches that hold water against the house or scrape the paint in wind.
Keep a phone note of anything you spot so it goes on the fall repair list.

sections.h2: Fall (October to November): repair and re-caulk
body: Fall is the most productive season for exterior work in our region: lower humidity, cooler surfaces, and fewer afternoon storms. This is the time to act on the list you built in spring and summer.
bullets: Cut out and replace cracked or shrunken caulk at windows, doors, trim joints, and siding butt joints using a quality exterior sealant.
Scrape, sand, and spot-prime small areas of peeling paint, then touch up with the original color.
Probe window sills, door jambs, and fascia ends with a screwdriver; soft wood needs replacement before painting.
Touch up the south and west elevations, which fade and chalk first.
If the house is due for a repaint, this is the start of the best season to schedule it.

sections.h2: Winter (December to February): plan and small fixes
body: Winter in North Central Florida usually leaves plenty of workable days, though early-morning dew and the occasional freeze mean you wait until surfaces are dry and above the minimum temperature on the product label. Use the season for planning and small jobs.
bullets: Re-read your notes and decide whether the next step is touch-ups or a full repaint.
Gather color ideas and get estimates early so work can begin before summer weather arrives.
Paint front doors, shutters, and railings on mild, dry days.
Check exterior lighting fixtures and hose bibs, where gaps let water into the wall.

body: How long a paint job lasts here depends on exposure, color, substrate, and the quality of the original prep. Our article on how long exterior paint lasts in Florida goes deeper, but the practical signal is simple: once touch-ups no longer blend, chalk rubs off heavily on your hand, or failures appear on several elevations at once, the coating is at the end of its life.

Scheduling a repaint on purpose, in the drier months, is very different from scrambling after rot has set in. When you plan ahead, you can choose the season, the colors, and the scope, and the prep stays focused on maintenance rather than repairs. A repaint should begin with a proper wash, repairs, caulking, and spot-priming, followed by two full coats of a 100% acrylic exterior paint, or an elastomeric system on stucco with hairline cracking.

sections.h2: Keep a simple log, and know when to call for help
body: The single most useful habit is writing down what you did and when: the date of the last wash, the caulk you used, the paint colors and products, and any spot that keeps failing. That log turns your next repaint into a planned project instead of an urgent one, and it makes any contractor's estimate more accurate.

Ground-level washing, caulking, and touch-ups are fine DIY tasks. Second-story work, rotten wood, and full repaints call for a crew with the right ladders, staging, and insurance. faqs.q: What month is best to paint a house exterior in North Central Florida?
faqs.a: October through May generally offers the best conditions, with lower humidity and fewer afternoon storms. Summer work is possible but needs early starts and careful attention to dew point and incoming rain.

faqs.q: How often should I re-caulk the outside of my house?
faqs.a: Inspect caulk every fall and replace any joints that are cracked, shrunken, or pulling away. Sun-facing joints usually fail first. Quality exterior sealants last several years, but inspection is cheaper than repairing rot.

faqs.q: Should I wash my house before or after pollen season?
faqs.a: After. Washing in late spring, once most of the pollen has dropped, removes it in one pass and gets the walls clean before summer humidity encourages mildew.

faqs.q: Can touch-ups replace a full repaint?
faqs.a: Touch-ups extend a paint job but cannot replace it forever. Once the paint chalks heavily, touch-ups stop blending, or failures show up on several sides of the house, a full repaint is the better value.
